claim: Influenza virus expresses transcripts early in infection and transitions towards genome replication at later time points.
source: Influenza virus expresses transcripts early in infection and transitions towards genome replication at later time points.
evidence: This is a general statement about influenza virus biology that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The transition from transcription to replication requires de novo assembly of the viral replication machinery, large ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs) composed of the viral polymerase, genomic RNA and oligomeric nucleoprotein (NP).
source: This process requires de novo assembly of the viral replication machinery, large ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs) composed of the viral polymerase, genomic RNA and oligomeric nucleoprotein (NP).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field of influenza virology.

claim: Human protein kinase C (PKC) family members regulate RNP assembly.
source: Here we demonstrate that human protein kinase C (PKC) family members regulate RNP assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental data including polymerase activity assays, co-immunoprecipitation experiments, and knockout studies.

claim: Activated PKCδ interacts with the polymerase subunit PB2.
source: Activated PKCδ interacts with the polymerase subunit PB2 and phospho-regulates NP oligomerization and RNP assembly during infection.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Activated PKCδ phospho-regulates NP oligomerization during infection.
source: Activated PKCδ interacts with the polymerase subunit PB2 and phospho-regulates NP oligomerization and RNP assembly during infection.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays, mass spectrometry data, and tail loop:groove interaction assays shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Knockout of PKCδ impairs virus infection by selectively disrupting genome replication.
source: Consistent with its role in regulating RNP assembly, knockout of PKCδ impairs virus infection by selectively disrupting genome replication.
evidence: This is supported by primer extension assays and replication assays in PKCδ knockout cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: Primary transcription from pre-formed RNPs deposited by infecting particles is unaffected by PKCδ knockout.
source: However, primary transcription from pre-formed RNPs deposited by infecting particles is unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by primer extension assays in PKCδ knockout cells treated with cycloheximide shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Influenza virus exploits host PKCs to regulate RNP assembly, a step required for the transition from primary transcription to genome replication during the infectious cycle.
source: Thus, influenza virus exploits host PKCs to regulate RNP assembly, a step required for the transition from primary transcription to genome replication during the infectious cycle.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined data from polymerase activity assays, knockout studies, and replication assays.

claim: NEP has been shown to shift the viral polymerase towards replication.
source: NEP has been shown to shift the viral polymerase towards replication; svRNAs are thought to associate with the viral polymerase and promote copying of full-length genomic RNA; and newly synthesized polymerase proteins have been proposed to stimulate replication in trans (Jorba et al., 2009; Perez et al., 2012, 2010; Robb et al., 2009; York et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: svRNAs are thought to associate with the viral polymerase and promote copying of full-length genomic RNA.
source: NEP has been shown to shift the viral polymerase towards replication; svRNAs are thought to associate with the viral polymerase and promote copying of full-length genomic RNA; and newly synthesized polymerase proteins have been proposed to stimulate replication in trans (Jorba et al., 2009; Perez et al., 2012, 2010; Robb et al., 2009; York et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Newly synthesized polymerase proteins have been proposed to stimulate replication in trans.
source: NEP has been shown to shift the viral polymerase towards replication; svRNAs are thought to associate with the viral polymerase and promote copying of full-length genomic RNA; and newly synthesized polymerase proteins have been proposed to stimulate replication in trans (Jorba et al., 2009; Perez et al., 2012, 2010; Robb et al., 2009; York et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The influenza virus RNP is a double helical structure containing the viral polymerase and repeating NP subunits coating each of the eight genomic RNAs.
source: The influenza virus RNP is a double helical structure containing the viral polymerase and repeating NP subunits coating each of the eight genomic RNAs (Arranz et al., 2012; Klumpp et al., 1997; Moeller et al., 2012; Pons et al., 1969).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The viral polymerase is a heterotrimer composed of the subunits PB1, PB2 and PA.
source: The viral polymerase, a heterotrimer composed of the subunits PB1, PB2 and PA, is located at one end of the RNP where it binds both the 5' and 3' genomic termini.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of influenza virology.

claim: The viral polymerase is located at one end of the RNP where it binds both the 5' and 3' genomic termini.
source: The viral polymerase, a heterotrimer composed of the subunits PB1, PB2 and PA, is located at one end of the RNP where it binds both the 5' and 3' genomic termini.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of influenza virology.

claim: Transcription of viral mRNAs occurs via a 'cap-snatching' mechanism.
source: Transcription of viral mRNAs occurs via a 'cap-snatching' mechanism, beginning immediately following nuclear import of the incoming RNPs and continuing throughout infection (Bouloy et al., 1978; Plotch et al., 1981).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Replication occurs at later time points when RNPs direct synthesis of a positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA) intermediate that templates replication of the negative-sense viral RNA genome (vRNA).
source: Replication occurs at later time points when RNPs direct synthesis of a positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA) intermediate that templates replication of the negative-sense viral RNA genome (vRNA) (Hay et al., 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Replication requires the assembly of RNPs containing newly synthesized polymerase, NP, and either cRNA (cRNPs) or vRNA (vRNPs).
source: Importantly, this replication requires the assembly of RNPs containing newly synthesized polymerase, NP, and either cRNA (cRNPs) or vRNA (vRNPs) (Barrett et al., 1979; Vreede et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NP forms homo-oligomers and binds RNA in a sequence-independent fashion to fully coat the genome.
source: To fully coat the genome, NP forms homo-oligomers and binds RNA in a sequence-independent fashion.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of influenza virology.

claim: NP oligomerizes spontaneously and binds non-specifically to cellular RNAs.
source: These same properties cause NP to oligomerize spontaneously and bind non-specifically to cellular RNAs (Baudin et al., 1994; Prokudina-Kantorovich and Semenova, 1996; Zhao et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Influenza virus NP oligomerizes by inserting a small 'tail loop' (aa 402–428) into the binding groove of a neighboring protomer.
source: Influenza virus NP oligomerizes by inserting a small 'tail loop' (aa 402–428) into the binding groove of a neighboring protomer (Ng et al., 2008; Ye et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A continuous supply of RNA-free monomeric NP is required for assembly into RNA-bound RNPs and replication of the viral genome.
source: NP binds RNA via a large basic surface and is thought to encapsidate the nascent RNA genome concomitant with its synthesis, hence a continuous supply of RNA-free monomeric NP is required for assembly into RNA-bound RNPs and replication of the viral genome (Beaton and Krug, 1986; Ng et al., 2008; Shapiro and Krug, 1988; Vreede et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and logical inference.

claim: Phosphorylation at the homotypic interface inhibits NP oligomerization during both influenza A and B virus replication.
source: We and others reported that phosphorylation at the homotypic interface inhibits NP oligomerization during both influenza A and B virus replication (Chenavas et al., 2013; Hutchinson et al., 2012; Mondal et al., 2015; Turrell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Phosphorylation or phospho-mimetics at residue S165 in the groove or S407 in the tail loop drives influenza A NP towards a monomeric state.
source: Specifically, phosphorylation or phospho-mimetics at residue S165 in the groove or S407 in the tail loop drives influenza A NP towards a monomeric state, prevents RNP assembly, and severely impairs viral replication (Mondal et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Phosphorylation at S165 or S407 prevents RNP assembly and severely impairs viral replication.
source: Specifically, phosphorylation or phospho-mimetics at residue S165 in the groove or S407 in the tail loop drives influenza A NP towards a monomeric state, prevents RNP assembly, and severely impairs viral replication (Mondal et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: NP mutants lacking key phospho-sites are defective in supporting influenza polymerase activity and virus replication.
source: NP mutants lacking key phospho-sites are also defective in supporting influenza polymerase activity and virus replication, and in some cases result in NP hyper-oligomerization (Mondal et al., 2015; Turrell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both hyper- and hypo-phosphorylation of NP is deleterious.
source: Thus, both hyper- and hypo-phosphorylation of NP is deleterious suggesting that the reversible phosphorylation of NP must be carefully balanced to enable recruitment of oligomerization-competent NP to sites of genome replication and ultimately incorporation into growing RNPs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature and the authors' own observations.

claim: Influenza virus does not encode a kinase.
source: Influenza virus does not encode a kinase, therefore the phospho-regulation of NP must be performed by host enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the influenza virus genome.

claim: The phospho-regulation of NP must be performed by host enzymes.
source: Influenza virus does not encode a kinase, therefore the phospho-regulation of NP must be performed by host enzymes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fact that influenza virus does not encode a kinase.

claim: Both activators and inhibitors of the PKC family have been shown to modulate influenza virus replication.
source: Both activators and inhibitors of the PKC family have been shown to modulate influenza virus replication (Hoffmann et al., 2008; Kistner et al., 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activating PKCs with phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA) stimulates NP phosphorylation and inhibits its oligomerization.
source: More recently we demonstrated that activating PKCs with phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA) stimulates NP phosphorylation and inhibits its oligomerization (Mondal et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The PKC family consists of at least eleven different members which can be divided into classical (α, β1, β2, γ), novel (δ, ε, η, θ) and atypical (ι/λ, ζ) isoforms based on their structure and co-factor requirements.
source: The PKC family consists of at least eleven different members which can be divided into classical (α, β1, β2, γ), novel (δ, ε, η, θ) and atypical (ι/λ, ζ) isoforms based on their structure and co-factor requirements.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PKC family.

claim: Expressing active PKCβ2, PKCδ, PKCθ and PKCη considerably reduced polymerase activity with respect to the empty vector control.
source: Expressing active PKCβ2, PKCδ, PKCθ and PKCη considerably reduced polymerase activity with respect to the empty vector control.
evidence: This is supported by the polymerase activity assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PKCβ2 and PKCη showed 60–80% decrease in polymerase activity.
source: While PKCβ2 and PKCη showed 60–80% decrease, PKCδ and PKCθ abrogated polymerase activity completely to background levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the polymerase activity assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PKCδ and PKCθ abrogated polymerase activity completely to background levels.
source: While PKCβ2 and PKCη showed 60–80% decrease, PKCδ and PKCθ abrogated polymerase activity completely to background levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the polymerase activity assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PKCε and PKCα showed moderate, but statistically significant reductions in polymerase activity.
source: PKCε and PKCα showed moderate, but statistically significant reductions, whereas the remaining isoforms caused minimal changes in polymerase activity, or even minor increases in activity.
evidence: This is supported by the polymerase activity assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Slower migrating forms of NP appeared in conditions where polymerase activity was inhibited.
source: Western blotting showed that slower migrating forms of NP appeared in conditions where polymerase activity was inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Slower migrating species of NP resulted from NP hyper-phosphorylation.
source: Phosphatase treatment confirmed that these slower migrating species resulted from NP hyper-phosphorylation and quantification revealed a strong correlation between increased NP phosphorylation and decreased polymerase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by phosphatase treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is a strong correlation between increased NP phosphorylation and decreased polymerase activity.
source: Phosphatase treatment confirmed that these slower migrating species resulted from NP hyper-phosphorylation and quantification revealed a strong correlation between increased NP phosphorylation and decreased polymerase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of NP phosphorylation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The inhibitory phenotype of PKC catalytic domains on polymerase activity was significantly reduced for inactive PKC mutants.
source: Whereas the catalytic domains of PKCβ2, PKCδ and PKCη inhibited polymerase activity, this phenotype was significantly reduced for the inactive mutants (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by polymerase activity assay data with inactive PKC mutants shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NP was not hyper-phosphorylated in the presence of inactive PKC mutants.
source: Moreover, NP was not hyper-phosphorylated in the presence of the inactive mutants, suggesting that specific PKC isoforms inhibit influenza polymerase activity by causing the phosphorylation of NP.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Specific PKC isoforms inhibit influenza polymerase activity by causing the phosphorylation of NP.
source: Moreover, NP was not hyper-phosphorylated in the presence of the inactive mutants, suggesting that specific PKC isoforms inhibit influenza polymerase activity by causing the phosphorylation of NP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that inactive PKC mutants do not cause NP hyper-phosphorylation or inhibit polymerase activity.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitations failed to detect stable interactions between NP and PKC when co-expressed in 293T cells.
source: Whereas NP is phosphorylated when PKCs are expressed and this correlates with the inhibitory phenotype, co-immunoprecipitations failed to detect stable interactions between NP and PKC when co-expressed in 293T cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NP was efficiently co-precipitated with catalytic fragments of PKCδ and PKCη when they were co-expressed with the other components of the RNP.
source: Surprisingly, NP was efficiently co-precipitated with catalytic fragments of PKCδ and PKCη when they were co-expressed with the other components of the RNP (i.e. viral polymerase and vRNA) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PKCβ2 co-precipitated only limited amounts of NP.
source: PKCβ2 co-precipitated only limited amounts of NP.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NP co-precipitated by PKCδ and PKCη was highly enriched for the hyper-phosphorylated form relative to its abundance in total cell lysate.
source: Notably, NP co-precipitated by PKCδ and PKCη was highly enriched for the hyper-phosphorylated form relative to its abundance in total cell lysate.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NP was co-precipitated by full-length PKC when the polymerase and vRNA were co-expressed.
source: Again, NP was co-precipitated by full-length PKC when the polymerase and vRNA were co-expressed.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NP showed a clear preference for interaction with PKCδ.
source: Additionally, NP showed a clear preference for interaction with PKCδ, although PKCη also co-precipitated minor amounts of NP.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Interactions between NP and PKC isoforms were enhanced in the presence of the viral polymerase and vRNA.
source: Interactions between NP and PKC isoforms were enhanced in the presence of the viral polymerase and vRNA (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The viral polymerase is sufficient to mediate the interaction between NP and PKC.
source: This enhanced interaction was still observed when the vRNA template was excluded from transfections or when RNaseA was included during the immunoprecipitation (not shown), suggesting that the viral polymerase is sufficient to mediate the interaction between NP and PKC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experiments where vRNA was excluded or RNaseA was added.

claim: Co-expression of PB2 alone was sufficient to ensure significant co-precipitation of NP by PKCδ.
source: Interestingly, co-expression of PB2 alone was sufficient to ensure significant co-precipitation of NP by PKCδ, whereas co-expression of PB1 and PA resulted in limited co-precipitation similar to that observed in the absence of the polymerase.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The oligomerization defective NP E339A was co-precipitated by PKCδ in the presence of PB2.
source: Furthermore, the oligomerization defective NP E339A was co-precipitated by PKCδ in the presence of PB2, suggesting NP monomers also participate in this interaction.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NP monomers participate in the interaction with PKCδ and PB2.
source: Furthermore, the oligomerization defective NP E339A was co-precipitated by PKCδ in the presence of PB2, suggesting NP monomers also participate in this interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that oligomerization-defective NP E339A is co-precipitated by PKCδ in the presence of PB2.

claim: PB2 bridged interactions between NP and the catalytic domains of PKCδ and PKCη.
source: PB2 bridged interactions between NP and the catalytic domains of PKCδ and PKCη.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the context of full length protein, PKCδ showed the strongest interactions with NP and PB2.
source: In the context of full length protein, PKCδ showed the strongest interactions with NP and PB2.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PB2 anchors a hetero-oligomeric NP:PB2:PKCδ complex.
source: Our data suggested that PB2 anchors a hetero-oligomeric NP:PB2:PKCδ complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing that PB2 bridges interactions between NP and PKCδ.

claim: NP present in the immuno-precipitated NP:PB2:PKCδ complex was significantly enriched for the hyper-phosphorylated form.
source: NP present in this immuno-precipitated complex was significantly enriched for the hyper-phosphorylated form, suggesting that PB2 facilitates a functional interaction between NP and activated PKC resulting in NP phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PB2 facilitates a functional interaction between NP and activated PKC resulting in NP phosphorylation.
source: NP present in this immuno-precipitated complex was significantly enriched for the hyper-phosphorylated form, suggesting that PB2 facilitates a functional interaction between NP and activated PKC resulting in NP phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that NP in the complex is enriched for the hyper-phosphorylated form.

claim: PKCβ2, PKCδ and PKCη phosphorylated NP in in vitro kinase assays.
source: All three PKC isoforms that inhibited polymerase activity, i.e. PKCβ2, PKCδ and PKCη, phosphorylated NP.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PKCε showed no specific kinase activity towards NP.
source: By contrast, PKCε, which exhibited modest inhibition of polymerase activity, showed no specific kinase activity and its activity was similar to that in the negative control.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The PKC inhibitor H7 almost completely eliminated NP phosphorylation in in vitro kinase assays.
source: H7 almost completely eliminated NP phosphorylation (Figure 3B), compared to the vehicle-only control that did not impact NP phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Select PKC isoforms, and not other fortuitously co-precipitating kinases, directly phosphorylated NP in vitro.
source: These kinase assays showed that select PKC isoforms, and not other fortuitously co-precipitating kinases, directly phosphorylated NP in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro kinase assay data and the specificity demonstrated by H7 inhibition.

claim: Phosphorylation of NP E339A was markedly increased by all three PKC isoforms compared to WT NP.
source: Compared to the WT NP control, phosphorylation of NP E339A was markedly increased by all three PKC isoforms, supporting a model where PKC targets sites at the NP:NP interface (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PKC targets sites at the NP:NP interface.
source: Compared to the WT NP control, phosphorylation of NP E339A was markedly increased by all three PKC isoforms, supporting a model where PKC targets sites at the NP:NP interface (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that monomeric NP E339A is phosphorylated more efficiently than WT NP.

claim: NP S165 and S407 are the crucial phospho-sites that regulate homo-oligomerization and RNP formation.
source: Our prior mutagenesis showed that NP S165 and S407 are the crucial phospho-sites that regulate homo-oligomerization and RNP formation (Mondal et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Phosphorylation was significantly reduced for NP S165A/S407A compared to the high levels detected for the monomer NP E339A.
source: Phosphorylation was significantly reduced for NP S165A/S407A compared to the high levels detected for the monomer NP E339A (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutation of NP S165 and S407 reduced phosphorylation by PKCδ and PKCη by almost 50%.
source: This defect was most pronounced for PKCδ and PKCη, where mutation of NP S165 and S407 reduced phosphorylation by almost 50% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), confirming that these sites are major targets for PKC-mediated phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NP S165 and S407 are major targets for PKC-mediated phosphorylation.
source: This defect was most pronounced for PKCδ and PKCη, where mutation of NP S165 and S407 reduced phosphorylation by almost 50% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), confirming that these sites are major targets for PKC-mediated phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that mutation of these sites significantly reduces phosphorylation.

claim: Residual phosphorylation detected on the NP S165A/S407A mutant may reflect phosphorylation at one of the other previously identified phospho-sites.
source: Residual phosphorylation detected on the NP S165A/S407A mutant may reflect phosphorylation at one of the other previously identified phospho-sites (Hutchinson et al., 2012; Mondal et al., 2015), and our quantitative mass spectrometry suggest that some of these sites could also be targets of PKCs (see below).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of residual phosphorylation and prior identification of other phospho-sites.

claim: Expression of PKCδ or PKCη severely reduced NP:NP interactions in the tail loop:groove interaction assay.
source: Expression of PKCδ or PKCη severely reduced NP:NP interactions and co-precipitation of NPΔTL.
evidence: This is supported by tail loop:groove interaction assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Loss of NP:NP interactions in the presence of PKCδ and PKCη was associated with the appearance of minor hyper-phosphorylated forms of NP.
source: Moreover, this loss of function in the presence of PKCδ and PKCη was again associated with the appearance of minor hyper-phosphorylated forms of NP.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Expression of PKCβ2 in cells did not change the amount of co-precipitated NPΔTL in the tail loop:groove interaction assay.
source: Whereas PKCβ2 can phosphorylate NP in an isolated kinase assay, expression of PKCβ2 in cells did not change the amount of co-precipitated NPΔTL.
evidence: This is supported by tail loop:groove interaction assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: NP:PA interactions were nearly eliminated when PKCδ was co-expressed in the RNP assembly assay.
source: NP was specifically co-precipitated by PA-FLAG, yet these interactions were nearly eliminated when PKCδ was co-expressed (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by RNP assembly assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Co-precipitation of the polymerase subunits PB1 and PB2 was unaffected by PKCδ expression in the RNP assembly assay.
source: Notably, co-precipitation of the other polymerase subunits PB1 and PB2 was unaffected by PKCδ expression, suggesting that phosphorylation by PKCδ selectively impairs RNP assembly but not polymerase trimer formation.
evidence: This is supported by RNP assembly assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Phosphorylation by PKCδ selectively impairs RNP assembly but not polymerase trimer formation.
source: Notably, co-precipitation of the other polymerase subunits PB1 and PB2 was unaffected by PKCδ expression, suggesting that phosphorylation by PKCδ selectively impairs RNP assembly but not polymerase trimer formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PKCδ impairs NP:PA interactions but not PB1:PA or PB2:PA interactions.

claim: PKCδ and PKCη disrupt influenza polymerase activity by phospho-regulating NP tail loop:grove interactions.
source: Together these results provide strong evidence that PKCδ and PKCη disrupt influenza polymerase activity by phospho-regulating NP tail loop:grove interactions, and thus have the potential to control NP oligomerization and RNP formation in cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data from polymerase activity assays, kinase assays, and tail loop:groove interaction assays.

claim: PKCδ is abundantly expressed in human lung tissue.
source: We focused on PKCδ given that NP exclusively interacts with full-length PKCδ (Figure 2B,D), PKCδ phospho-regulates NP oligomerization and RNP assembly (Figure 3), and that PKCδ is abundantly expressed in human lung tissue, typical sites of influenza virus replication, and the human lung epithelial A549 cells used here (Goldberg and Steinberg, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Endogenous PKCδ specifically co-precipitated with PB2-FLAG during infection.
source: Endogenous PKCδ specifically co-precipitated with PB2-FLAG (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from infected cells shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PB2 specifically co-precipitated with endogenous PKCδ during infection.
source: The reciprocal immunoprecipitation performed on infected cell lysates showed a similar interaction; PB2 specifically co-precipitated with endogenous PKCδ, compared to background amounts precipitated by a non-specific control (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from infected cells shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PB2 complexes purified from infected cell lysate contained PKC-specific kinase activity.
source: In vitro kinase assays performed with immuno-precipitated PB2 complexes revealed specific phosphorylation of NP, which was eliminated when the PKC inhibitor H7 was included in the reaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data with immunoprecipitated PB2 complexes shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Treatment of the immunoprecipitated PB2 complex with RNase A markedly increased NP phosphorylation.
source: Moreover, treatment of the immunoprecipitated complex with RNase A markedly increased phosphorylation, suggesting that the lower-order NP released by RNase A treatment rather than the oligomerized RNA-associated form was a better substrate for the kinase activity associated with the complex.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lower-order NP released by RNase A treatment is a better substrate for the kinase activity associated with the PB2 complex than the oligomerized RNA-associated form.
source: Moreover, treatment of the immunoprecipitated complex with RNase A markedly increased phosphorylation, suggesting that the lower-order NP released by RNase A treatment rather than the oligomerized RNA-associated form was a better substrate for the kinase activity associated with the complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that RNase A treatment increases NP phosphorylation.

claim: PB2 is associated with activated PKCδ during infection.
source: Note that these kinase reactions did not include any exogenous second messenger activators of PKC, suggesting that PB2 is associated with activated PKCδ.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that kinase activity is present without exogenous activators.

claim: PKCδ is activated during influenza infection.
source: Phospho-proteomics provided further evidence that PKCδ is activated during influenza. We identified peptides from PKCδ containing phosphorylated serines at residues 302 and 304 (Table 1), an autocatalytic marker of PKCδ activation (Durgan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-proteomic data identifying phosphorylation at S302 and S304 shown in Table 1, and citation to prior literature identifying these as activation markers.

claim: Phosphorylation of PKCδ at serines 302 and 304 is an autocatalytic marker of PKCδ activation.
source: We identified peptides from PKCδ containing phosphorylated serines at residues 302 and 304 (Table 1), an autocatalytic marker of PKCδ activation (Durgan et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PKCδ protein expression was completely abolished in the PRKCD knockout cells.
source: PKCδ protein expression was completely abolished in the knockout cells, while very low levels of PKCβ2 were detected by the cross-reactive antibody (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NP phosphorylation was considerably reduced in the PRKCD−/− cells compared to WT cells.
source: Compared to the WT cells, NP phosphorylation was considerably reduced in the PRKCD−/− cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Phosphorylation at NP S165 and S407 decreased by 60–80% in PRKCD−/− cells.
source: This was especially true at the key regulatory positions of NP S165 and S407, where phosphorylation levels decreased by 60–80%.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The relative abundance of phosphorylation at T378 in the body was only marginally affected in PRKCD−/− cells.
source: By contrast, the relative abundance of phosphorylation at T378 in the body was only marginally affected.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PKCδ is an important kinase targeting phospho-regulatory sites at the site of NP:NP interface.
source: These data illustrate that PKCδ is an important kinase targeting phospho-regulatory sites at the site of NP:NP interface.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mass spectrometry data showing reduced phosphorylation at S165 and S407 in PKCδ knockout cells.

claim: There is functional redundancy for NP phosphorylation, possibly fulfilled by other PKC isoforms.
source: However, as phosphorylation was not completely ablated in the absence of PKCδ, these results also suggest at least some functional redundancy for NP phosphorylation, possibly fulfilled by other PKC isoforms.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that phosphorylation is reduced but not eliminated in PKCδ knockout cells.

claim: Viral gene expression was reduced by ~60% in the PRKCD−/−−1 cell line and ~30% in the PRKCD−/−−2 line for both WSN and CA04 reporter viruses.
source: Gene expression was reduced for both viruses by ~60% in the PRKCD−/−−1 cell line and ~30% in the PRKCD−/−−2 line (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by reporter virus gene expression data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Gene expression from a West Nile virus replicon did not differ significantly between WT and PKCδ knockout cells.
source: This PKCδ-dependent defect was not simply a generic reduction in viral entry or gene expression, as gene expression from a West Nile virus replicon did not differ significantly between WT and knockout cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by West Nile virus replicon gene expression data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Entry of the pseudotyped influenza virus or bona fide vesicular stomatitis virus was similar in the presence or absence of PKCδ.
source: Flow cytometry confirmed that entry of the pseudotyped influenza virus or bona fide vesicular stomatitis virus was similar in the presence or absence of PKCδ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Influenza gene expression was impaired in the knockout cell lines even with the pseudotyped FVG-R virus.
source: Even with the pseudotyped FVG-R virus, influenza gene expression was impaired in the knockout cell lines, indicating that PKCδ is important post-entry for gene expression and genome replication independent of its role in influenza virus entry (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by reporter virus gene expression data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PKCδ is important post-entry for gene expression and genome replication independent of its role in influenza virus entry.
source: Even with the pseudotyped FVG-R virus, influenza gene expression was impaired in the knockout cell lines, indicating that PKCδ is important post-entry for gene expression and genome replication independent of its role in influenza virus entry (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that gene expression is impaired even when entry is bypassed.

claim: The kinetics of NP nuclear import and subsequent export to the cytoplasm were unchanged in infected PRKCD−/− cells.
source: Nonetheless, immunofluorescence assays showed that the kinetics of NP nuclear import and subsequent export to the cytoplasm were unchanged in infected PRKCD−/− cells, although total NP levels might be reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Production of normal influenza virus in the knockout cell lines was reduced by up to 1000 fold in a single-cycle infection.
source: Compared to WT cells, production of normal influenza virus in the knockout cell lines was reduced by up to 1000 fold in a single-cycle infection, consistent with the decreases in viral gene expression observed with our reporter viruses (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by single-cycle replication data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Viral titers were reduced by over 1.5 logs in both PRKCD−/− cell lines compared to the sgRNA control line in a multi-cycle replication assay.
source: However, viral titers were reduced by over 1.5 logs in both PRKCD−/− cell lines compared to the sgRNA control line in a multi-cycle replication assay (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by multi-cycle replication data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Phosphorylation of NP by endogenous PKCδ is crucial for viral gene expression, production of infectious progeny and multi-cycle replication.
source: Together, these data establish that phosphorylation of NP by endogenous PKCδ is crucial for viral gene expression, production of infectious progeny and multi-cycle replication.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data showing reduced gene expression and replication in PKCδ knockout cells.

claim: Reductions in replication in PKCδ knockout cells likely represent combined effects of PKCδ knockout on both viral gene expression and entry.
source: These reductions in replication likely represent combined effects of PKCδ knockout on both viral gene expression and entry (see below).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed effects on both entry and gene expression.

claim: Additional PKC family members or other host kinases play secondary or redundant roles in regulating NP phosphorylation.
source: As viral gene expression and replication was not completely abolished in the absence of PKCδ, they also implicate additional PKC family members or other host kinases as playing secondary or redundant roles in regulating NP phosphorylation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that gene expression and replication are reduced but not eliminated in PKCδ knockout cells.

claim: Knockout of PKCδ reduced virion attachment or uptake ~2 fold.
source: Knockout of PKCδ reduced virion attachment or uptake ~2 fold (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by entry assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Attachment and entry were indistinguishable for all cell lines in the acid bypass assay.
source: Attachment and entry were indistinguishable for all cell lines in the acid bypass assay (Figure 6A), indicating that the lack of PKCδ does not alter attachment or pH-dependent fusion, but rather endosome-mediated uptake.
evidence: This is supported by acid bypass entry assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The lack of PKCδ does not alter attachment or pH-dependent fusion, but rather endosome-mediated uptake.
source: Attachment and entry were indistinguishable for all cell lines in the acid bypass assay (Figure 6A), indicating that the lack of PKCδ does not alter attachment or pH-dependent fusion, but rather endosome-mediated uptake.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that acid bypass normalizes entry across all cell lines.

claim: PKCδ is one of the isoforms involved in endosome-mediated uptake during infection.
source: Entry assay results agreed with prior reports showing that PKC inhibitors and mutants interfere with entry and trap influenza virions in the late endosome, suggesting that PKCδ is one of the isoforms involved in these early steps during infection (Root et al., 2000; Sieczkarski et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the entry assay data and citations to prior literature.

claim: PKCδ knockout cell lines showed a significant reduction in viral gene expression at both 8 and 24 hr post-inoculation when infections were initiated via acid bypass.
source: PKCδ knockout cell lines showed a significant reduction in viral gene expression at both 8 and 24 hr post-inoculation compared to parental A549 cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by replication assay data with acid bypass shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PKCδ directly impacts gene expression and possibly genome replication during infection.
source: Thus, PKCδ directly impacts gene expression and possibly genome replication during infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that gene expression is reduced even when entry is bypassed.

claim: vRNA and mRNA levels were similar in WT and PRKCD−/− cells during primary transcription.
source: vRNA and mRNA levels were similar in WT and PRKCD−/− cells, providing evidence that PKCδ is not required for nuclear import or primary transcription of incoming vRNPs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by primer extension assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PKCδ is not required for nuclear import or primary transcription of incoming vRNPs.
source: vRNA and mRNA levels were similar in WT and PRKCD−/− cells, providing evidence that PKCδ is not required for nuclear import or primary transcription of incoming vRNPs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that vRNA and mRNA levels are similar during primary transcription.

claim: cRNA levels were decreased by over 80% in PKCδ knockout cells compared to the parental during replication.
source: cRNA levels were decreased by over 80% in knockout cells compared to the parental, indicating dramatic defects in genome replication.
evidence: This is supported by primer extension assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: vRNA and mRNA levels were reduced by about 50% in PKCδ knockout cells during replication.
source: vRNA and mRNA levels were reduced by about 50%.
evidence: This is supported by primer extension assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PKCδ plays an important role enabling genome replication and secondary transcription.
source: Thus, PKCδ plays an important role enabling genome replication and secondary transcription, events that both require formation of new RNPs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that replication and secondary transcription are impaired in PKCδ knockout cells.

claim: Dynamic phosphorylation establishes a localized pool of monomeric NP that is essential for forming nascent RNPs and the transition to genome replication.
source: Both hyper-phosphorylation by PKC over-expression or hypo-phosphorylation by PKCδ knockout or NP mutation disrupt the balance of NP oligomerization (Mondal et al., 2015), leading us to propose that dynamic phosphorylation establishes a localized pool of monomeric NP that is essential for forming nascent RNPs and the transition to genome replication (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their combined data.

claim: Additional factors, possibly cellular phosphatases, may be required to license NP oligomerization and initiate genome replication.
source: This raises the possibility that additional factors, possibly cellular phosphatases, may be required to license NP oligomerization and initiate genome replication.
evidence: This is speculation based on the model that NP must be licensed for oligomerization.

claim: Protein phosphatase 6 was reported to directly bind multiple subunits of the viral polymerase and regulate RNA synthesis during infection.
source: Protein phosphatase 6 was reported to directly bind multiple subunits of the viral polymerase and regulate RNA synthesis during infection, although it is not known if it targets any of these proteins for dephosphorylation (York et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Influenza virus deploys multiple approaches to ensure temporally regulated transcription and replication of the viral genome.
source: Thus, influenza virus deploys multiple approaches to ensure temporally regulated transcription and replication of the viral genome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data and prior literature showing multiple regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Influenza virus infection triggers multiple kinase cascades including phosphoinositide 3 kinase (PI3K), the Raf/MEK/ERK pathway, c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNK) and PKCs.
source: Influenza virus infection triggers multiple kinase cascades including phosphoinositide 3 kinase (PI3K), the Raf/MEK/ERK pathway, c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNK) and PKCs (Planz, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PKCα has been shown to phosphorylate PB1-F2 at sites that are important for viral replication.
source: Another family member, PKCα, has also been shown to phosphorylate PB1-F2 at sites that are important for viral replication (Mitzner et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In vitro assays have suggested that PKCα phosphorylates PB1 and NS1.
source: In vitro assays have suggested that PKCα phosphorylates PB1 and NS1 (Mahmoudian et al., 2009), although our cell-based assays did not demonstrate any significant regulatory role for PKCα on polymerase function.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Genetic ablation of PKCδ or PKCβ2 activity reduced viral entry.
source: Genetic ablation of PKCδ or PKCβ2 activity reduced viral entry, possibly by perturbing endosomal sorting and maturation (Figure 6 and (Sieczkarski et al., 2003)).
evidence: This is supported by entry assay data shown in Figure 6 and citation to prior literature.

claim: Broad-spectrum PKC inhibitors may be especially effective anti-viral compounds.
source: The involvement of multiple PKC isoforms at multiple stages during infection suggests that broad-spectrum PKC inhibitors may be especially effective anti-viral compounds, even at concentrations that do not fully block PKC activity or their normal cellular functions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that multiple PKC isoforms are involved at multiple stages of infection.

claim: PKCs have been shown to regulate gene expression and replication of other negative-strand RNA viruses by phosphorylating their P proteins.
source: This may extend beyond influenza virus, as PKCs have been shown to regulate gene expression and replication of other negative-strand RNA viruses by phosphorylating their P proteins, including human parainfluneza virus 3, Sendai virus, and rabies virus (De et al., 1995; Gupta et al., 2000; Huntley et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: S165 in the NP groove lies within a linear consensus recognition motif for PKCs, RxxS.
source: S165 in the NP groove lies within a linear consensus recognition motif for PKCs, RxxS, where arginine at the −3 position facilitates kinase-substrate interactions (Nishikawa et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Both NP R162 and S165 in the PKC recognition motif are highly conserved in influenza A viruses.
source: Both NP R162 and S165 in the PKC recognition motif are highly conserved in influenza A viruses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza A virus NP sequences.

claim: NP S403 lies within a PKC recognition motif, although the phospho-site and recognition motif are not well conserved.
source: NP S403 also lies within a PKC recognition motif, although the phospho-site and recognition motif are not well conserved.
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence analysis.

claim: NP residues S402, S407 and S413 do not reside within linear motifs and may rely on structure-based recognition motifs formed by non-contiguous regions of the protein.
source: In contrast, other residues including S402, S407 and S413 do not reside within linear motifs and may rely on structure-based recognition motifs formed by non-contiguous regions of the protein (Duarte et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of linear recognition motifs and citation to prior literature on structure-based recognition.

claim: PKC and PKA family members often rely upon additional co-factors to phosphorylate target proteins.
source: While kinase recognition motifs help to establish a specific kinase-substrate interaction, PKC and PKA family members often rely upon additional co-factors to phosphorylate target proteins (Mochly-Rosen and Gordon, 1998; Welch et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PKCs pair with anchoring proteins, collectively termed receptor of activated C-kinase (RACKs), to enhance kinase activity and stability, increase their affinity and selectivity towards specific substrates, and integrate multiple signaling pathways.
source: PKCs pair with anchoring proteins, collectively termed receptor of activated C-kinase (RACKs), to enhance kinase activity and stability, increase their affinity and selectivity towards specific substrates, and integrate multiple signaling pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKC regulation.

claim: PB2 performs an analogous function to RACKs by anchoring PKCδ and NP.
source: Our data suggest that PB2 performs an analogous function anchoring PKCδ and NP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing PB2 bridges interactions between PKCδ and NP.

claim: PB2 anchors PKCδ and NP through non-overlapping protein-protein interactions.
source: Like RACKs, PB2 anchors PKCδ and NP through non-overlapping protein-protein interactions; PB2 helps to convey specificity, preferentially interacting with full-length PKCδ compared to full-length PKCβ2 or PKCη; and PB2 anchors activated PKCδ as evidenced by kinase activity in in vitro reactions without the need for exogenous activators (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation and kinase assay data.

claim: PB2 helps to convey specificity, preferentially interacting with full-length PKCδ compared to full-length PKCβ2 or PKCη.
source: Like RACKs, PB2 anchors PKCδ and NP through non-overlapping protein-protein interactions; PB2 helps to convey specificity, preferentially interacting with full-length PKCδ compared to full-length PKCβ2 or PKCη; and PB2 anchors activated PKCδ as evidenced by kinase activity in in vitro reactions without the need for exogenous activators (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Binding to PB2 might activate or stabilize the activated conformation of PKCδ.
source: It is tempting to speculate that binding to PB2 might activate or stabilize the activated conformation of PKCδ, as has been shown for other RACK:PKC pairings (Mochly-Rosen and Gordon, 1998), or provide increased recognition of the non-canonical site at S407.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to other RACK:PKC interactions.

claim: The polymerase itself, or perhaps just the PB2 subunit alone, may contribute to the PKC-mediated phospho-regulation of RNP assembly.
source: It thus appears that the polymerase itself, or perhaps just the PB2 subunit alone, may contribute to the PKC-mediated phospho-regulation of RNP assembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that PB2 anchors PKCδ and NP.

claim: The PB2-phosphoNP complexes may function in cis to regulate the initial stages of RNP assembly or possibly in trans to shuttle monomeric NP to already growing RNPs.
source: The PB2-phosphoNP complexes may function in cis to regulate the initial stages of RNP assembly or possibly in trans to shuttle monomeric NP to already growing RNPs, analogous to the role of the phosphoprotein P from non-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses that chaperones monomeric nucleocapsid proteins to replicating RNPs (Masters and Banerjee, 1988).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to other viral systems.

claim: NP must ultimately be licensed for oligomerization to form an RNP.
source: It is not known how NP is recruited to the growing oligomer chain, but regardless of the route of recruitment, NP must ultimately be licensed for oligomerization to form an RNP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model that NP phosphorylation inhibits oligomerization.

claim: Licensing NP for oligomerization may involve altered PB2:PKC and PB2:NP interactions, changes to the activation state of PKCδ associated with PB2, or possibly the involvement of cellular phosphatases.
source: This adds another layer of control, and may involve altered PB2:PKC and PB2:NP interactions, changes to the activation state of PKCδ associated with PB2, or possibly the involvement of cellular phosphatases.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms for licensing NP oligomerization.

claim: Both over expression and knockout of PKCδ perturb RNP formation.
source: As both over expression and knockout of PKCδ perturb RNP formation, it is clear that the activity of PKCs must be finely balanced to enable NP oligomerization when and where it is needed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data showing that both hyper- and hypo-phosphorylation are deleterious.

claim: The activity of PKCs must be finely balanced to enable NP oligomerization when and where it is needed.
source: As both over expression and knockout of PKCδ perturb RNP formation, it is clear that the activity of PKCs must be finely balanced to enable NP oligomerization when and where it is needed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data showing that both hyper- and hypo-phosphorylation are deleterious.
